title: Asking permission
hookLine: a young woman brings a complaint about her own father's arrangement

cards: A woman comes to the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, with a complaint about her own father. He has married her to a man, and she didn't want it. Sahih al-Bukhari keeps her name: Khansa' bint Khidham.
Her case comes down to a plain question: does a marriage made over her refusal stand? The father has made his decision. And she has come to the one person whose answer will settle it.

teach.h: KHANSA' SAID NO. IT WAS ANNULLED.
teach.b: The report in Bukhari, in paraphrase: her father married her off while she disliked it, she came to the Messenger of Allah, and he annulled the marriage. A father's arrangement didn't override her refusal.
Second, the rule behind the story.
Another hadith in Bukhari, in paraphrase: a woman who has been married before is not to be married until she is consulted, and a woman who has never married, not until her permission is asked.
The companions asked: how is her permission given? In one version, 'A'ishah adds: but she is shy. And the Prophet answered: her silence.
That's a careful detail. Silence isn't the goal. The hadith makes room for a shy bride without letting anyone skip her.

teach.h: SHE IS ASKED, EVEN IF SHY.
teach.b: She is asked, and her answer, even a quiet one, is the answer. And Khansa's story shows that a clear no ends it. Third, the word.

teach.h: IDHN: PERMISSION, AS AT A DOOR.
teach.b: In Arabic, permission is idhn. Think of a door. In surah al-Nur, the Qur'an says, in paraphrase, that if you find no one home, you don't go in until you've been given permission.
A marriage, like a house, isn't entered without being let in. Fourth, the schools.

teach.h: THE SCHOOLS DIFFER; SHE IS ASKED.
teach.b: Muslim scholars discuss the role of the bride's guardian, the wali, and the schools differ on the details. But beneath the details, these two hadith hold one line in place: she is asked, and her answer counts.

how: Muslims cite these hadith for a bride's consent: she is asked before the contract, and the schools set out the role of her guardian, the wali, in different ways.

o: asking the imam's leave before holding a wedding at the mosque
a couple asking their parents' blessing after the wedding
a bride is asked before her marriage, and her no is honored

s: in Khansa's case, her father's arrangement stood over her refusal
Khansa' refused, came to the Prophet, and he annulled the marriage.
the hadith makes room for a shy bride
asked how her permission is given, the Prophet answered: her silence.
only a woman married before has to be asked
both are asked: one is consulted, the other's permission is sought.

games.q: you're Khansa' bint Khidham. your father has married you to a man you didn't want. what do you do?
o: go to the Prophet and tell him.
games.why: she went to the Prophet, and he annulled the marriage. her refusal was the answer.

practice: Think of a decision coming up that touches someone else: a plan you'd make for them, a photo you'd post of them, a favor you'd volunteer them for.
Picture yourself asking first, then waiting for the answer without leaning on it: a question, and a pause long enough for the reply.

wordCard.voice: Asking permission. A bride is asked before her marriage, and her no is honored. Today's word.

carryVoice: Your line: her consent. Even a shy yes is hers to give. That one's in the books.

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 5138 (Khansa' bint Khidham, married against her will; the marriage annulled)
Sahih al-Bukhari 5136, 5137 (consulted / permission asked; 'her silence'; 'A'ishah: she is shy)
Qur'an 24:28 (do not enter until permission is given)
